summary: A 1974 note describing proposed changes to the ARPANET IMP and the way hosts connect to it. It covers decoupling the message numbering of different hosts, host-to-host access control, a message number window, and handling messages outside the normal mechanism. It points to BBN Report 1822 for the interface itself.

plainLanguage.summary: This note announces four planned changes to the ARPANET's IMP software. The changes separate host conversations, add permission checks, allow more messages in flight, and support a limited experimental packet type.

subtitle: Four planned changes to ARPANET message handling and the IMP/Host interface.

tldr.problem: Hosts sharing two IMPs also shared a four-message window, so one host pair could affect another. The interface also lacked access checks and a way to send experimental packets outside normal sequencing.
tldr.mechanism: The note announces separate host-pair message sequences, an access check, a window increased from four to eight messages, and a special single-packet type that bypasses sequencing and retransmission.
tldr.outcome: The changes were announced as backward compatible, with possible minor timing differences. The special packet facility was to be restricted by the Network Control Center.

sections.title: Four Planned Interface Changes
sections.content:
RFC 660 announces changes to the IMP software and the IMP/Host interface described in BBN Report 1822. The four areas are host-to-host message numbering, access control, the message window, and a special message outside the normal mechanism.

The note says the changes are backward compatible, although timing may differ slightly. It asks readers to keep the note with their copy of BBN Report 1822 until that report is updated.
sections.plainLanguage: The network's IMPs are getting four interface changes. The note says existing hosts should continue to work, though timing may shift slightly.

sections.title: Separate Sequences and Access Checks
sections.content:
Previously, four outstanding messages between a pair of IMPs were shared by every host pair attached to those IMPs. The planned change gives each host pair a separate message-number sequence, selected dynamically from a limited pool. If many conversations exhaust the pool, it is shared over time; none is stopped, though all may slow.

The IMPs will also check administrative permission when hosts try to communicate after two minutes without communication. Initially, the default allows all hosts. A denied pair receives a Destination Dead Message with sub-code 3. The outstanding-message window grows from four to eight.
sections.plainLanguage: Each pair of hosts gets its own message count, reducing interference. The IMP also checks permission after a quiet period and can allow up to eight outstanding messages per pair.

sections.title: The Special Single-Packet Message
sections.content:
Specified hosts may use new type 3 for limited experiments that do not need the normal ordered, error-controlled sequence. The source IMP accepts only a single-packet message of this type; a multi-packet message is discarded.

The packet travels by normal routing and may arrive out of order. The destination IMP puts it directly on the host output queue, without reassembly, retransmission, RFNMs, or incomplete-transmission handling. If resources are insufficient, it is discarded. The Network Control Center regulates which hosts may use this facility because uncontrolled use could harm network performance.
sections.plainLanguage: This experimental packet can arrive out of order or be discarded. It skips retries and reassembly, so only approved hosts may use it.
